lead: A spanning tree keeps every vertex of a connected graph, uses exactly n − 1 edges, and has no cycle. Among all spanning trees of a weighted graph, the minimum spanning tree (MST) has the smallest total edge weight. Real networks — cables, roads, water pipes, circuit tracks — must join every point at least cost. Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms find an MST greedily by taking a cheapest safe edge; both rely on the cut property.
prereq: You need: 6.1 for vertices and edges, 6.8 for tree properties, and 6.7 for weighted graphs.

blocks.text: Take a connected graph G = (V, E) with n = |V| vertices and m = |E| edges. A spanning tree of G is a subgraph T that keeps every vertex, is connected, and has no cycle. By 6.8, T has exactly n − 1 edges.

Every connected graph has at least one spanning tree. While a cycle exists, delete any edge of that cycle; the graph stays connected because the rest of the cycle still links the two ends. Repeat until no cycle remains. This deletes m − n + 1 edges, the cycle rank. A disconnected graph has a spanning forest, one tree per component.
Fibre plans, road plans, and Ethernet's spanning tree protocol all pick one spanning tree so every site is reached and no redundant loop remains.

sections.h3: Minimum spanning tree and the cut property

blocks.text: In a weighted graph each edge e has weight w(e): metres, rupees, milliseconds. The weight of a spanning tree T is the sum of its edge weights. An MST is a spanning tree of smallest possible weight.
w(T) = Σ w(e) for e in T
blocks.where: w(T) is the total weight of T; w(e) is the weight of edge e; the sum runs over the n − 1 edges of T.

blocks.text: A cut splits V into two non-empty sets S and V − S. An edge crosses the cut when its ends lie on opposite sides. Cut property: a lightest edge crossing any cut belongs to some MST; if it is the unique lightest edge across that cut, it belongs to every MST. Greedy choices therefore never block a cheaper finish.

Mirror rule: the heaviest edge of a cycle, when strictly heavier than every other edge of that cycle, lies in no MST. Both facts follow by an exchange argument: swap the edge for a cheaper one and keep a spanning tree of smaller weight.
Kruskal builds the tree from a sorted edge list.

items: Sort all m edges by weight, smallest first.
Start with T empty. Each of the n vertices is its own component.
Walk the sorted list. For edge (u, v), add it only if u and v are in different components, then merge those components. Otherwise skip it: it would close a cycle.
Stop when T has n − 1 edges, or when the list ends.

blocks.text: Component tests use union-find. find(x) gives x's component label; union joins two labels. Each test is almost constant time, so sorting dominates: O(m log m). Kruskal suits sparse graphs and edge lists. In Figure 1, AC (3) is skipped because A and C are already joined through B.
Prim grows one tree from a start vertex r.

items: Put S = {r}, the vertices already in the tree, and T empty.
While S ≠ V, take a cheapest edge with one end in S and one end outside S. Add it to T and add its outside end to S.
When S = V, T is an MST with n − 1 edges.

blocks.text: Each chosen edge is a lightest edge across (S, V − S), so it is safe by the cut property. An array key[] stores the cheapest known edge from each outside vertex into S, and a min-heap picks the next vertex: O(m log n). With an adjacency matrix and a scan it is O(n²), good for dense graphs.
The total weight is the sum of the n − 1 chosen weights. The start vertex changes the order, not the total. Ties allow several MSTs with the same minimum weight.

items: Cayley's formula: n vertices give n<sup>n−2</sup> labelled trees, so 5 vertices give 5<sup>3</sup> = 125.
Kruskal is edge-first; Prim is vertex-first; both return an MST of the same minimum total weight.

figure.caption: Edges BC (1), AB (2), DE (2) and BD (4) form the minimum spanning tree, total weight 9. The lighter skipped edges were never needed.

spec.aria: A weighted graph on five vertices A to E; the four bold edges BC 1, AB 2, DE 2 and BD 4 form a minimum spanning tree of total weight 9.

examples.question: Figure 1 has vertices A, B, C, D, E and edges AB 2, AC 3, BC 1, BD 4, CD 5, CE 6, DE 2, BE 7. (a) Run Kruskal's algorithm and list chosen edges with total weight. (b) Confirm with Prim's algorithm from A.
steps: Sorted: BC 1, AB 2, DE 2, AC 3, BD 4, CD 5, CE 6, BE 7.
n = 5, so a spanning tree needs 4 edges.
BC (1): B and C are separate, add it. Weight = 1.
AB (2): A alone, B with C, add it. T = {BC, AB}, weight = 3.
DE (2): D and E separate, add it. Weight = 5.
AC (3): A and C are both in {A, B, C}, skip it — it would close A–B–C–A.
BD (4): {A, B, C} and {D, E} differ, add it. T = {BC, AB, DE, BD}, weight = 9, four edges, stop.
Prim from A: S = {A}; cut edges AB 2, AC 3, take AB 2. Weight = 2.
S = {A, B}; cut edges AC 3, BC 1, BD 4, BE 7, take BC 1. Weight = 3.
S = {A, B, C}; cut edges BD 4, CE 6, BE 7, take BD 4. Weight = 7.
S = {A, B, C, D}; cut edges DE 2, CE 6, BE 7, take DE 2. Weight = 9.
examples.answer: Kruskal chooses BC (1), AB (2), DE (2) and BD (4); total weight 9. Prim from A chooses the same four edges with total 9.
examples.check:
edges = [(1,'B','C'),(2,'A','B'),(2,'D','E'),(3,'A','C'),(4,'B','D'),(5,'C','D'),(6,'C','E'),(7,'B','E')]
parent = {v: v for v in 'ABCDE'}
def find(x):
    while parent[x] != x:
        parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]
        x = parent[x]
    return x
total = 0
count = 0
for w, u, v in sorted(edges):
    ru, rv = find(u), find(v)
    if ru != rv:
        parent[ru] = rv
        total += w
        count += 1
print(total)
print(count)

traps: Kruskal must test for a cycle before adding: a cheap edge such as AC (3) is skipped when its ends already sit in one component.
Stop at n − 1 edges. Adding a fifth edge to a spanning tree of 5 vertices always creates a cycle.
Prim's total weight is the same for every start vertex; only the order of chosen edges changes. Do not restart Prim at each vertex and add totals.
When weights tie, several MSTs exist with the same total weight. Questions asking 'the MST' usually want any one of them plus the total.
An MST minimises total weight, not the distance between two particular vertices. A shortest path between two vertices need not lie inside the MST (see 6.7).

quiz.q: Define a spanning tree of a connected graph with n vertices, and state how many edges it has.
quiz.a: A subgraph that contains all n vertices, is connected, and has no cycle. It has exactly n − 1 edges.

quiz.q: State the cut property of minimum spanning trees.
quiz.a: For any cut (S, V − S), a lightest edge crossing the cut belongs to some MST; if it is the unique lightest crossing edge, every MST contains it.

quiz.q: Why does Kruskal's algorithm skip an edge whose two ends are already in the same component?
quiz.a: That component already has a path between the ends, so adding the edge closes a cycle and the result would not be a tree. Skipping keeps the chosen set acyclic while it grows to n − 1 edges.

quiz.q: A graph has vertices P, Q, R, S with edges PQ 1, QR 2, RS 3, PR 4, PS 5. Run Kruskal's algorithm and give the chosen edges and total weight.
quiz.a: Sorted: PQ 1, QR 2, RS 3, PR 4, PS 5. Add PQ (1), QR (2), RS (3). PR is skipped because P and R are already joined; PS is skipped because all vertices are joined. Three edges for four vertices. Total = 1 + 2 + 3 = 6.

quiz.q: Run Prim's algorithm from vertex E on the graph of Figure 1. Give the chosen edges in order and the total weight.
quiz.a: S = {E}: cut edges DE 2, CE 6, BE 7, take DE 2. S = {D, E}: cut edges BD 4, CD 5, CE 6, BE 7, take BD 4. S = {B, D, E}: cut edges AB 2, BC 1, AC 3, CD 5, CE 6, BE 7, take BC 1. S = {B, C, D, E}: cut edges AB 2, AC 3, take AB 2. Total = 2 + 4 + 1 + 2 = 9.

quiz.q: All edge weights in a connected weighted graph are distinct. Show that the MST is unique.
quiz.a: Suppose two different MSTs T1 and T2 exist. Pick an edge e in T1 but not in T2. Removing e from T1 splits its vertices into S and V − S, and e is the unique lightest edge crossing that cut. By the cut property every MST must contain e, contradicting e not being in T2. So only one MST exists.

quiz.q: A graph is disconnected. What does Kruskal's algorithm return, and how does the stopping rule change?
quiz.a: It returns a minimum spanning forest, one tree per connected component with least possible weight. The rule 'stop at n − 1 edges' becomes 'stop when the edge list ends', and the result has n − c edges where c is the number of components.

beyond: Not for the exam. Minimum spanning trees drive single-linkage clustering: build the MST of a distance graph and cut its longest edges to get clusters. Doubling an MST and taking shortcuts gives a 2-approximation for the travelling salesman problem. MSTs also generate mazes, plan circuit tracks, and guide image segmentation. The cut property generalises to matroids, where the same greedy rule solves a whole family of optimisation problems. Search 'MST clustering', 'Christofides algorithm' and 'graphic matroid' to go further.
